pqdoctor: Overview
(A command-line tool that checks whether a server negotiates post-quantum TLS, works out why not, and prints the fix.)
pqdoctor answers one question about a TLS server: is it post-quantum, and if not, why? It sends seven hand-built ClientHellos, reads only the server’s first reply to each, and turns the replies into a verdict, a stable cause code, and the fix for that server’s software.

npm install -g pqdoctor

Prebuilt for Windows, macOS (Apple silicon and Intel) and Linux (x86_64 and arm64), from npm.

Install pqdoctor 0.4.0
Quickstart
pqdoctor nginx.org
✘ nginx.org:443 (3.147.99.198)

Not post-quantum: TLS 1.2 only

The server doesn't speak TLS 1.3, so it can't do hybrid ML-KEM.

cause: tls12-only server: nginx/1.31.3

Fixes

1. Turn on TLS 1.3

Hybrid post-quantum key exchange only exists in TLS 1.3. This server answered with TLS 1.2.

# nginx

ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;

# Apache

SSLProtocol -all +TLSv1.2 +TLSv1.3

2. nginx: link against OpenSSL 3.5+ and list the PQ group

nginx gets PQ from its TLS library. OpenSSL 3.5 or newer is needed (Ubuntu 25.04+, Debian 13+, or an nginx build linked against 3.5). Check with `nginx -V`.

ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;

ssl_ecdh_curve X25519MLKEM768:X25519:prime256v1;

pqdoctor: Where else it runs
(A command-line tool that checks whether a server negotiates post-quantum TLS, works out why not, and prints the fix.)
The same Rust engine is inside Flarebox, the GitHub Action, and the checker on Try it, which runs on Cloudflare’s network. All of them give the same verdict, cause and fix for the same server.

How it works: Overview
(Seven hand-made ClientHellos, read only up to the server's first reply, turned into a verdict, a cause and a fix.)
pqdoctor asks one question of a TLS server: does it negotiate hybrid post-quantum key exchange (X25519MLKEM768, codepoint 0x11EC)? If it doesn’t, the useful part is why, because each reason has a different fix.

To find out, it sends seven ClientHellos it builds by hand and reads only the server’s first reply to each: a ServerHello, a HelloRetryRequest, or an alert. It never completes a handshake for these probes and never sends application data.

How it works: The seven probes
(Seven hand-made ClientHellos, read only up to the server's first reply, turned into a verdict, a cause and a fix.)
# | Probe | What it shows
1 | TLS 1.3 with classical groups | The baseline: does TLS 1.3 work at all, and which group does the server pick?
2 | Offer only an X25519MLKEM768 key share | Does it accept post-quantum when that’s all there is, or ask for something else?
3 | X25519 share, ML-KEM listed first | Does it prefer PQ, asking a client that sent only an X25519 share to retry with ML-KEM?
4 | Old draft group X25519Kyber768Draft00 | Does it only know the pre-standard Kyber draft?
5 | PQ ClientHello split across two TCP segments | A real PQ hello is large and often split. Does something in the path drop it?
6 | Classical ClientHello, same size, split | The control for 5: is it the size and split, or the PQ group itself?
7 | P-256 / P-384 only | Does the server only answer NIST curves, a sign of a hand-written curve list?
The probes run one at a time, 120 ms apart, with 5 s connect and read timeouts. A probe that gets no reply is retried once. Parallel probes trip servers’ rate limiters: an early version fired all seven at once, www.debian.org rate-limited the burst, and pqdoctor reported “No TLS handshake at all”. It was confidently wrong, so the probes became sequential and “nothing answered” became its own verdict.

How it works: From replies to a cause
(Seven hand-made ClientHellos, read only up to the server's first reply, turned into a verdict, a cause and a fix.)
The replies are read in a fixed order. The first rule that matches gives the verdict and the cause code:

Couldn’t connect: connect-failed.

Neither a classical nor a P-curve hello got any TLS answer, only timeouts or resets: no-reply. pqdoctor doesn’t guess here, since the server may be down, firewalled or rate-limiting.

Probe 2 got a post-quantum group: post-quantum. It’s pq-preferred if probe 3 got a retry request for ML-KEM, pq otherwise, and pq-split-dropped if probe 5 went unanswered.

No hello completed with any group: no-tls.

The server answered TLS 1.2: tls12-only.

Classical TLS 1.3 works but the PQ hello dies: large-hello-dropped if the same-size classical hello (probe 6) also dies, pq-group-rejected if only the PQ group does.

Probe 4 got the Kyber draft group: kyber-draft-only.

Otherwise, TLS 1.3 without ML-KEM: pinned-nist if the server steers X25519 clients to P-256 or only answers P-curve hellos, no-mlkem if not.

How it works: Tailoring the fix
(Seven hand-made ClientHellos, read only up to the server's first reply, turned into a verdict, a cause and a fix.)
A fix depends on the server software. pqdoctor makes one plain-HTTP HEAD / on port 80 and reads the Server header (3 s, best effort). From it, it picks a stack: nginx, Apache, HAProxy, Caddy, IIS, Node, Java, envoy and others, and Postfix, Dovecot, Exim or Exchange from a mail server’s greeting. The fixes are then written for that stack, and there’s always a Cloudflare Tunnel fallback. --no-http skips the request.

How it works: The certificate check
(Seven hand-made ClientHellos, read only up to the server's first reply, turned into a verdict, a cause and a fix.)
After the key-exchange probes, pqdoctor checks post-quantum authentication: does the server serve an ML-DSA certificate? This needs to read the Certificate message, which TLS 1.3 encrypts, so it’s the one place pqdoctor does real cryptography. It completes one X25519 exchange and runs the TLS 1.3 key schedule (AES-128-GCM) just far enough to decrypt the Certificate and CertificateVerify, then hangs up. It never sends Finished. That’s two more connections. It’s on by default for a single host and off for scans (--auth turns it on).

How it works: Every address
(Seven hand-made ClientHellos, read only up to the server's first reply, turned into a verdict, a cause and a fix.)
A name with several addresses can have servers that disagree. For one host, pqdoctor checks every address the name resolves to, up to six, and reports per address when they differ. The fix lab has a localhost case answering classical on 127.0.0.1 and post-quantum on ::1. --first-address checks only the first.

How it works: Being polite
(Seven hand-made ClientHellos, read only up to the server's first reply, turned into a verdict, a cause and a fix.)
Handshake-only: no application data is ever sent.

The Server header request’s User-Agent names the tool and can carry a contact (--contact) for opt-outs.

scan runs at most 4 hosts at once and starts at most 2 new hosts a second by default (caps: 32 and 20). Each host’s probes stay one at a time.

--exclude FILE skips hosts and their subdomains.

Reading a report: Overview
(What each part of a pqdoctor report means, using real output for github.com, cloudflare.com and nginx.org.)
All output on this page is real, from 2026-10-15. Servers change, so running it today may give different answers.

Reading a report: The verdict
(What each part of a pqdoctor report means, using real output for github.com, cloudflare.com and nginx.org.)
The first lines say what was checked, the verdict, why, and the cause code:

pqdoctor github.com
✘ github.com:443 (140.82.114.4)

Not post-quantum

TLS 1.3 works, but when offered X25519MLKEM768 the server asks for X25519 instead. Its TLS library doesn't have ML-KEM, or the groups are limited in config.

cause: no-mlkem

✔ means post-quantum and ✘ means it isn’t. The address in brackets is the one that was probed.

The cause code is stable, so it’s what scans, the GitHub Action and Flarebox’s history compare. The sentence above it can change between versions.

When the Server header names the software, it’s shown next to the cause, e.g. server: nginx/1.31.3. That’s what tailors the fixes.

A post-quantum server looks like this. It has more than one address, so each is listed:

pqdoctor cloudflare.com
✔ cloudflare.com:443 (104.16.133.229)

Post-quantum: negotiates X25519MLKEM768

Supports and prefers hybrid ML-KEM key exchange.

cause: pq-preferred server: cloudflare

Addresses

· 104.16.133.229 pq-preferred · X25519MLKEM768

· 104.16.132.229 pq-preferred · X25519MLKEM768

Reading a report: Mixed
(What each part of a pqdoctor report means, using real output for github.com, cloudflare.com and nginx.org.)
From 0.4.0, a non-PQ answer is checked again: the same address, key exchange only, 1 s later (--reprobe N for up to N re-checks, at most 5; --reprobe 0 turns it off). If any re-check negotiates ML-KEM, the verdict is mixed, marked ◐: “Mixed: post-quantum on some connections, not on others”. A warning says how many of the checks were post-quantum, and with which group.

It means the servers behind that one address don’t all agree. That’s typical of a provider rolling ML-KEM out to some of its servers at a time: on 2026-10-26, 14 of the study’s 15 “regressions” were Google Cloud pools mid-rollout, answering post-quantum on 3 to 7 of 11 probes to the same address. It isn’t a regression, and it’s post-quantum once every server is.

The exit status is 1, since it isn’t fully post-quantum.

pqdoctor diff lists a host that went from post-quantum to mixed under mixed, not regressed, and exits 0 for it. Mixed back to post-quantum is fixed.

The agent, the fleet and the GitHub Action’s fail-on: regression don’t count it as a regression either.

Every re-check is in the JSON report’s reprobes.

Reading a report: Fixes
(What each part of a pqdoctor report means, using real output for github.com, cloudflare.com and nginx.org.)
Fixes are numbered in the order to try them. The first is for the stack pqdoctor found, the last is always the Cloudflare Tunnel fallback, and each has the config lines to paste:

pqdoctor nginx.org
✘ nginx.org:443 (3.147.99.198)

Not post-quantum: TLS 1.2 only

The server doesn't speak TLS 1.3, so it can't do hybrid ML-KEM.

cause: tls12-only server: nginx/1.31.3

Fixes

1. Turn on TLS 1.3

Hybrid post-quantum key exchange only exists in TLS 1.3. This server answered with TLS 1.2.

# nginx

ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;

# Apache

SSLProtocol -all +TLSv1.2 +TLSv1.3

2. nginx: link against OpenSSL 3.5+ and list the PQ group

nginx gets PQ from its TLS library. OpenSSL 3.5 or newer is needed (Ubuntu 25.04+, Debian 13+, or an nginx build linked against 3.5). Check with `nginx -V`.

ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;

ssl_ecdh_curve X25519MLKEM768:X25519:prime256v1;

3. Can't upgrade? Cloudflare Tunnel

Run cloudflared next to the server. The tunnel from the server to Cloudflare already uses post-quantum key agreement, so the hop that leaves your network is protected even if the server isn't.

cloudflared tunnel run <tunnel-name>

Reading a report: Authentication
(What each part of a pqdoctor report means, using real output for github.com, cloudflare.com and nginx.org.)
The ML-DSA check lists the certificate chain the server sends today’s clients: each certificate’s key, what signed it, and its size. Then it says whether the server serves an ML-DSA certificate:

pqdoctor github.com (continued)
Authentication No ML-DSA certificate

Leaf: ec-p256 key, signed ecdsa-sha256. Listing ML-DSA schemes doesn't break it, and offered only ML-DSA it refuses cleanly — what any correct TLS stack does, so this doesn't show whether its stack could serve ML-DSA. The chain is 2737 bytes.

ml-dsa: no-cert

leaf github.com ec-p256 signed ecdsa-sha256 1009 B

↑ Sectigo Public Server Authenticat… ec-p256 signed ecdsa-sha384 867 B

↑ Sectigo Public Server Authenticat… ec-p384 signed ecdsa-sha384 842 B

Reading a report: Probes
(What each part of a pqdoctor report means, using real output for github.com, cloudflare.com and nginx.org.)
Each of the seven probes, with the server’s first reply and how long it took:

pqdoctor github.com (continued)
Probes

· TLS 1.3 with classical groups TLS 1.3: picked X25519 (57 ms)

· Offer only an X25519MLKEM768 key share TLS 1.3: asked to retry with X25519 (58 ms)

· X25519 share, ML-KEM listed first TLS 1.3: picked X25519 (53 ms)

· Old draft group X25519Kyber768Draft00 TLS 1.3: asked to retry with X25519 (52 ms)

· PQ ClientHello split across two TCP segments TLS 1.3: asked to retry with X25519 (89 ms)

· Classical ClientHello, same size, split TLS 1.3: picked X25519 (103 ms)

· P-256 / P-384 only TLS 1.3: picked P-256 (56 ms)

Read across, these tell the story: TLS 1.3 works (1), offered only ML-KEM the server asks for X25519 instead (2), and it doesn’t know the Kyber draft either (4). Split hellos are fine (5, 6), so no middlebox is at fault, and it answers P-curves (7) without preferring them. So it’s no-mlkem, not pinned-nist.

Reading a report: Verify it yourself
(What each part of a pqdoctor report means, using real output for github.com, cloudflare.com and nginx.org.)
Every report ends with an OpenSSL command that offers only X25519MLKEM768. With OpenSSL 3.5+, a post-quantum server’s handshake completes with that group, and any other server’s fails:

openssl s_client -connect github.com:443 -servername github.com -groups X25519MLKEM768 </dev/null 2>&1 | grep -i 'group'

Reading a report: JSON
(What each part of a pqdoctor report means, using real output for github.com, cloudflare.com and nginx.org.)
--json prints the whole report as one object. These are the fields that matter for automation:

Field
verdict | pq, pqWithWarning, notPq, noTls13, broken, unreachable or, from 0.4.0, mixed
causeCode | The cause code
group | The PQ group negotiated, if any
prefersPq | Picks ML-KEM even when the client’s first key share is classical
warnings | E.g. split PQ hellos dropped, or PQ only when offered first
fixes | title, detail and snippet for each fix
fingerprint | serverHeader, stack, TLS version, cipher
probes | Each probe and its reply
auth | The certificate check, when it ran
addresses | Per-address results, when the name has more than one
reprobes | 0.4.0: the re-checks after a non-PQ answer, when there were any
verify | The OpenSSL command

Reading a report: Exit status
(What each part of a pqdoctor report means, using real output for github.com, cloudflare.com and nginx.org.)
For one host: 0 post-quantum, 1 not post-quantum (including mixed), 2 unreachable or an error.

The QUIC check (0.2.0): quic-pq-preferred, quic-pq, quic-no-mlkem, quic-hello-rejected, quic-no-reply, quic-version.

Causes and fixes: Fixes by server
(Every cause code pqdoctor reports, what it means, how often the study found it, and where the fix is.)
The config lines for each server, and the Tunnel fallback, are on Fixes by server.

no-mlkem: Overview
(TLS 1.3 works, but the server has no ML-KEM. The most common cause by far.)
TLS 1.3 works, but the server doesn’t negotiate ML-KEM. Either its TLS library is too old to have it, or the group list in its config leaves it out.

This was 61.3% of the non-post-quantum origins in the study: 2,108 of 3,439.

no-mlkem: How pqdoctor sees it
(TLS 1.3 works, but the server has no ML-KEM. The most common cause by far.)
The classical TLS 1.3 hello (probe 1) gets a ServerHello.

Offered only an X25519MLKEM768 key share (probe 2), the server asks the client to retry with a classical group, usually X25519.

It doesn’t steer clients to NIST curves. That would be pinned-nist.

no-mlkem: Shown in the fix lab
(TLS 1.3 works, but the server has no ML-KEM. The most common cause by far.)
The fix lab ran real servers with this fault. pqdoctor reported each one not post-quantum, and the fix it printed made each one post-quantum:

Server | Fix applied | After
OpenSSL 3.5, groups X25519:P-256 | ssl_ecdh_curve X25519MLKEM768:X25519:prime256v1 | PQ
Node, ecdhCurve set to X25519 | ecdhCurve: 'X25519MLKEM768:X25519:P-256' | PQ
Go without ML-KEM (GODEBUG=tlsmlkem=0, pre-1.24 behaviour) | Go 1.24+ defaults (CurvePreferences = nil) | PQ
Go with CurvePreferences X25519, P-256 | Remove CurvePreferences | PQ
SMTP, IMAP STARTTLS with pinned groups | The Postfix / Dovecot group list | PQ

no-mlkem: In the study
(TLS 1.3 works, but the server has no ML-KEM. The most common cause by far.)
Server software named in the Server header for no-mlkem origins: unknown 1,030, nginx 600, apache 225, aws 151, envoy 30. The header is often missing, so “unknown” is large.

no-mlkem: Verify
(TLS 1.3 works, but the server has no ML-KEM. The most common cause by far.)
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com -groups X25519MLKEM768 </dev/null 2>&1 | grep -i 'group'

tls12-only: Overview
(The server doesn't speak TLS 1.3, so it can't do hybrid ML-KEM at all.)
The server answers with TLS 1.2. Hybrid post-quantum key exchange only exists in TLS 1.3, so nothing else matters until TLS 1.3 is on.

This was 33.3% of the non-post-quantum origins in the study: 1,146 of 3,439.

tls12-only: How pqdoctor sees it
(The server doesn't speak TLS 1.3, so it can't do hybrid ML-KEM at all.)
Every probe, even the classical TLS 1.3 one, gets a TLS 1.2 ServerHello. Real output for nginx.org on 2026-10-15:

pqdoctor nginx.org (probes)
Probes

· TLS 1.3 with classical groups TLS 1.2 ServerHello (78 ms)

· Offer only an X25519MLKEM768 key share TLS 1.2 ServerHello (76 ms)

· X25519 share, ML-KEM listed first TLS 1.2 ServerHello (77 ms)

· Old draft group X25519Kyber768Draft00 TLS 1.2 ServerHello (80 ms)

· PQ ClientHello split across two TCP segments TLS 1.2 ServerHello (117 ms)

· Classical ClientHello, same size, split TLS 1.2 ServerHello (121 ms)

· P-256 / P-384 only TLS 1.2 ServerHello (82 ms)

tls12-only: The fix
(The server doesn't speak TLS 1.3, so it can't do hybrid ML-KEM at all.)
Turn on TLS 1.3, then add the PQ group:

# nginx

ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;

ssl_ecdh_curve X25519MLKEM768:X25519:prime256v1;

# Apache

SSLProtocol -all +TLSv1.2 +TLSv1.3

SSLOpenSSLConfCmd Groups X25519MLKEM768:X25519:prime256v1

The TLS library underneath has to be OpenSSL 3.5 or newer for the group to exist. Every server is on Fixes by server.

tls12-only: Shown in the fix lab
(The server doesn't speak TLS 1.3, so it can't do hybrid ML-KEM at all.)
An OpenSSL 3.5 server capped at TLS 1.2 was reported tls12-only. After enabling TLS 1.3 (ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3) and the groups line, it was post-quantum.

Separately, OpenSSL requiring TLS 1.3 got a protocol_version alert from all three tls12-only sites in the 60-site comparison: nginx.org, www.mit.edu and www.baidu.com.

tls12-only: Many are redirectors
(The server doesn't speak TLS 1.3, so it can't do hybrid ML-KEM at all.)
Many tls12-only hosts are bare domains (the Tranco entry), not the site people visit. Among the first 300 origins, the study probed the www. names of 51 TLS 1.2 apexes. For 22 of them, www. was on a CDN (Akamai 13, CloudFront 6, Cloudflare 3): the apex is a leftover redirect server in front of a CDN-hosted site.

That host still terminates TLS for everyone who types the bare domain, so it’s a real gap, and a cheap one to fix. It also means the headline percentage partly measures redirectors.

tls12-only: In the study
(The server doesn't speak TLS 1.3, so it can't do hybrid ML-KEM at all.)
Server header for tls12-only origins: unknown 491, nginx 315, aws 177, apache 134, iis 23.

large-hello-dropped: Overview
(Classical hellos work, but anything the size of a post-quantum ClientHello, split across packets, dies in the path.)
A classical hello works, but any ClientHello padded to post-quantum size and split across packets fails. Something in the path can’t reassemble a ClientHello that spans TCP segments: a load balancer, WAF or firewall that inspects TLS.

The verdict is broken, not just “not post-quantum”. Real browsers send hellos this size today, so these clients may already be failing.

This was 32 of the 3,439 non-post-quantum origins in the study (0.9%).

large-hello-dropped: How pqdoctor sees it
(Classical hellos work, but anything the size of a post-quantum ClientHello, split across packets, dies in the path.)
The classical TLS 1.3 hello (probe 1) works.

The PQ hello (probe 2) fails.

The control, a classical hello of the same size split the same way (probe 6), fails too. So it’s the size and the split, not the PQ group. If probe 6 worked, the cause would be pq-group-rejected.

large-hello-dropped: The fix
(Classical hellos work, but anything the size of a post-quantum ClientHello, split across packets, dies in the path.)
Update or replace the middlebox. Check every load balancer, WAF and firewall that inspects TLS in front of the server. Update its firmware, or turn off TLS inspection for this traffic.

pqdoctor also prints the stack’s upgrade fix, since the server behind the box may need it too.

large-hello-dropped: Shown in the fix lab
(Classical hellos work, but anything the size of a post-quantum ClientHello, split across packets, dies in the path.)
A post-quantum OpenSSL 3.5 server behind a box that drops ClientHellos over 1,200 bytes was reported “Breaks on PQ”. With the box removed, it was post-quantum.

large-hello-dropped: In the study
(Classical hellos work, but anything the size of a post-quantum ClientHello, split across packets, dies in the path.)
Server header: nginx 21, unknown 9, apache 2.

pq-split-dropped: Overview
(Post-quantum, but a PQ ClientHello split across two TCP segments gets no answer.)
The server is post-quantum, but a PQ ClientHello split across two TCP segments gets no answer. Real clients’ PQ hellos are often split, so something in the path, usually a load balancer or firewall, will fail some of them.

The verdict is pqWithWarning: post-quantum, with this warning in the report.

pq-split-dropped: How pqdoctor sees it
(Post-quantum, but a PQ ClientHello split across two TCP segments gets no answer.)
The PQ hello in one piece (probe 2) negotiates X25519MLKEM768.

The same hello split across two segments (probe 5) gets no reply.

pq-split-dropped: The fix
(Post-quantum, but a PQ ClientHello split across two TCP segments gets no answer.)
Find the device in front of the server that can’t reassemble a split ClientHello, and update it or turn off its TLS inspection for this traffic.

pq-split-dropped: Shown in the fix lab
(Post-quantum, but a PQ ClientHello split across two TCP segments gets no answer.)
A post-quantum OpenSSL 3.5 server behind a box that drops ClientHellos split across TCP segments was reported “PQ + warning”. With the box removed, it was post-quantum with no warning.

pq-split-dropped: From Workers
(Post-quantum, but a PQ ClientHello split across two TCP segments gets no answer.)
The checker on Cloudflare’s network writes the two halves 40 ms apart, but whether they leave Cloudflare’s network as separate TCP segments can’t be observed locally. So this warning may not reproduce from Workers.

pq-group-rejected: Overview
(Same-size classical hellos are fine, but offering the X25519MLKEM768 codepoint breaks the handshake.)
Same-size classical hellos are fine, but offering X25519MLKEM768 breaks the handshake. Something doesn’t tolerate a key-share group it doesn’t know. A correct stack ignores an unknown group and picks one it knows.

The verdict is broken. In the study, 2 of 3,439 non-post-quantum origins.

pq-group-rejected: How pqdoctor sees it
(Same-size classical hellos are fine, but offering the X25519MLKEM768 codepoint breaks the handshake.)
The classical TLS 1.3 hello (probe 1) works.

The PQ hello (probe 2) fails.

The same-size classical hello split the same way (probe 6) works, so size isn’t the problem. The codepoint is.

pq-group-rejected: The fix
(Same-size classical hellos are fine, but offering the X25519MLKEM768 codepoint breaks the handshake.)
Find what chokes on the X25519MLKEM768 codepoint (0x11EC). It’s usually an old TLS-inspecting appliance, or a TLS library with a key-share parsing bug. Update it.

pq-group-rejected: Shown in the fix lab
(Same-size classical hellos are fine, but offering the X25519MLKEM768 codepoint breaks the handshake.)
A post-quantum OpenSSL 3.5 server behind a box that resets on the X25519MLKEM768 codepoint was reported “Breaks on PQ”. With the box removed, it was post-quantum.

pq-other-group: Overview
(Post-quantum, but only with a group other than X25519MLKEM768 — so most clients still get a classical key exchange.)
0.2.0
This cause code is new in pqdoctor 0.2.0. It comes from the group survey, which is on by default for one host and --groups for scans. Without the survey, such a server is reported as no-mlkem.

The server does post-quantum key exchange, just not with X25519MLKEM768. Offered only SecP256r1MLKEM768, SecP384r1MLKEM1024 or a pure ML-KEM group, it picks it. But browsers, Go, OpenSSL and rustls send X25519MLKEM768, so in practice they negotiate a classical group.

The verdict is pqWithWarning (exit status 0), with group set to the group it accepts and a warning to add X25519MLKEM768.

pq-other-group: How pqdoctor sees it
(Post-quantum, but only with a group other than X25519MLKEM768 — so most clients still get a classical key exchange.)
The “PQ only” probe (an X25519MLKEM768 share, with X25519 and P-256 also listed) gets a retry to a classical group.

In the survey, a hello offering only SecP256r1MLKEM768 (say) gets a ServerHello that picks it.

This is what a server looks like whose groups were set for CNSA 2.0 or FIPS (NIST curves only), or whose TLS stack shipped the NIST-curve hybrids first.

pq-other-group: The fix
(Post-quantum, but only with a group other than X25519MLKEM768 — so most clients still get a classical key exchange.)
Put X25519MLKEM768 first and keep the group you have:

ssl_ecdh_curve X25519MLKEM768:SecP256r1MLKEM768:X25519:prime256v1;

SSLOpenSSLConfCmd Groups X25519MLKEM768:SecP256r1MLKEM768:X25519:prime256v1

pqdoctor fix --config PATH does this for you for nginx, Apache, HAProxy, Postfix and Dovecot.

kyber-draft-only: Overview
(The server only knows the pre-standard X25519Kyber768Draft00 group, which browsers have dropped.)
The server supports the pre-standard Kyber draft group, but not final ML-KEM. It only knows X25519Kyber768Draft00 (0x6399), which browsers have dropped.

In the study, 1 of 3,439 non-post-quantum origins.

kyber-draft-only: How pqdoctor sees it
(The server only knows the pre-standard X25519Kyber768Draft00 group, which browsers have dropped.)
The Kyber draft hello (probe 4) gets X25519Kyber768Draft00. The ML-KEM hello (probe 2) doesn’t get a post-quantum group.

kyber-draft-only: The fix
(The server only knows the pre-standard X25519Kyber768Draft00 group, which browsers have dropped.)
Move from the Kyber draft to final ML-KEM. Upgrade the TLS library to one with X25519MLKEM768 (0x11EC). pqdoctor also prints the upgrade fix for the stack it finds.

(The server only knows the pre-standard X25519Kyber768Draft00 group, which browsers have dropped.)
No maintained TLS stack still ships X25519Kyber768Draft00 alone, so there’s no real server to test against. This cause is covered by unit tests only.

pinned-nist: Overview
(TLS 1.3 without ML-KEM, and the server prefers NIST P-curves. Almost always a hand-written curve list.)
TLS 1.3 works, but the server only negotiates NIST P-curves and prefers them over X25519. That’s almost always a hand-set curve list that leaves out X25519MLKEM768, or a TLS library too old to have it.

This was 3.2% of the non-post-quantum origins in the study: 109 of 3,439.

pinned-nist: How pqdoctor sees it
(TLS 1.3 without ML-KEM, and the server prefers NIST P-curves. Almost always a hand-written curve list.)
A client offering an X25519 key share is asked to retry with P-256 or P-384, or

only the P-256 / P-384 hello (probe 7) completes.

pinned-nist: The fix
(TLS 1.3 without ML-KEM, and the server prefers NIST P-curves. Almost always a hand-written curve list.)
Put X25519MLKEM768 at the front of the hand-set list:

# Apache (mod_ssl on OpenSSL 3.5+)

SSLOpenSSLConfCmd Groups X25519MLKEM768:X25519:prime256v1

# nginx

ssl_ecdh_curve X25519MLKEM768:X25519:prime256v1;

The TLS library still has to have ML-KEM (OpenSSL 3.5+). Every server is on Fixes by server.

pinned-nist: Shown in the fix lab
(TLS 1.3 without ML-KEM, and the server prefers NIST P-curves. Almost always a hand-written curve list.)
An OpenSSL 3.5 server with groups pinned to P-256:P-384 was reported not post-quantum. After the Apache snippet’s Groups X25519MLKEM768:X25519:prime256v1, it was post-quantum. A POP3 STARTTLS server pinned the same way was fixed by the Dovecot list.

pinned-nist: In the study
(TLS 1.3 without ML-KEM, and the server prefers NIST P-curves. Almost always a hand-written curve list.)
Server header for pinned-nist origins: unknown 83, nginx 9, iis 7, aws 5, apache 4.

no-tls, no-reply, connect-failed: Overview
(When pqdoctor can't get a TLS answer, it says so instead of guessing.)
These three causes mean pqdoctor couldn’t get far enough to say anything about post-quantum. It reports that plainly rather than guessing.

no-tls, no-reply, connect-failed: no-tls
(When pqdoctor can't get a TLS answer, it says so instead of guessing.)
TLS alerts to every hello, including the classical and P-curve ones. Verdict noTls13: “No TLS handshake at all”. Common reasons are that the port isn’t TLS, or the server needs a different SNI name.

In the study: 41 of 3,439 non-post-quantum origins (1.2%).

no-tls, no-reply, connect-failed: no-reply
(When pqdoctor can't get a TLS answer, it says so instead of guessing.)
Only timeouts or resets, with no TLS alert at all. Verdict unreachable: “No reliable reply”. The server may be down, behind a firewall, or rate-limiting repeated connections. Re-check in a minute.

This verdict exists because of a mistake. An early version fired its probes in parallel, and www.debian.org rate-limited the burst, so pqdoctor said “No TLS handshake at all”. That was confidently wrong. Now the probes run one at a time, a silent probe is retried once, and silence is reported as silence.

no-tls, no-reply, connect-failed: connect-failed
(When pqdoctor can't get a TLS answer, it says so instead of guessing.)
The TCP connection couldn’t be opened. Verdict unreachable: “Couldn’t reach host:port”. In a multi-address report, an address that’s unreachable from this machine (for example, IPv6 with no IPv6 route) is marked as such, not as a disagreement.

no-tls, no-reply, connect-failed: In the study
(When pqdoctor can't get a TLS answer, it says so instead of guessing.)
523 of the 5,139 probed origins gave no TLS answer on port 443. They’re left out of every share, which is why the denominator is 4,616.

Fixes by server: Overview
(The exact config lines pqdoctor prints for nginx, Apache, HAProxy, Caddy, Node, Go, IIS, Java, mail servers, and the Cloudflare Tunnel fallback.)
pqdoctor reads the Server header (or a mail server’s greeting) to pick the fix. These are the lines it prints, word for word.

What the fix lab proves
The group strings for nginx, Apache, Node, Postfix and Dovecot go through the same OpenSSL call (SSL_CTX_set1_groups_list) that those servers use, on real OpenSSL 3.5 servers. Each one made the server post-quantum (30 / 30). The nginx, Apache, HAProxy, Postfix, Dovecot and Exim binaries themselves weren’t run: they need Linux. Go was run for real (Go 1.25).

Hybrid post-quantum needs TLS 1.3, and a TLS library that has ML-KEM: OpenSSL 3.5+, current BoringSSL and AWS-LC, Go 1.24+, or rustls with aws-lc-rs.

Fixes by server: Apache
(The exact config lines pqdoctor prints for nginx, Apache, HAProxy, Caddy, Node, Go, IIS, Java, mail servers, and the Cloudflare Tunnel fallback.)
Needs mod_ssl built against OpenSSL 3.5 or newer (httpd -V, openssl version).

SSLProtocol -all +TLSv1.2 +TLSv1.3

SSLOpenSSLConfCmd Groups X25519MLKEM768:X25519:prime256v1

Fixes by server: HAProxy
(The exact config lines pqdoctor prints for nginx, Apache, HAProxy, Caddy, Node, Go, IIS, Java, mail servers, and the Cloudflare Tunnel fallback.)
Use HAProxy built with OpenSSL 3.5+ or AWS-LC (haproxy -vv).

haproxy.cfg
global

ssl-default-bind-curves X25519MLKEM768:X25519:P-256

Fixes by server: Caddy
(The exact config lines pqdoctor prints for nginx, Apache, HAProxy, Caddy, Node, Go, IIS, Java, mail servers, and the Cloudflare Tunnel fallback.)
Go 1.24 offers X25519MLKEM768 by default. Upgrade Caddy and remove any custom curves option, or add x25519mlkem768 to it.

Caddyfile
tls {

curves x25519mlkem768 x25519 secp256r1

}

Fixes by server: Node.js
(The exact config lines pqdoctor prints for nginx, Apache, HAProxy, Caddy, Node, Go, IIS, Java, mail servers, and the Cloudflare Tunnel fallback.)
Check node -p process.versions.openssl. It must be 3.5 or newer.

https.createServer({ ...opts, ecdhCurve: 'X25519MLKEM768:X25519:P-256' }, app)

Fixes by server: Go
(The exact config lines pqdoctor prints for nginx, Apache, HAProxy, Caddy, Node, Go, IIS, Java, mail servers, and the Cloudflare Tunnel fallback.)
Go 1.24+ includes X25519MLKEM768 by default. If CurvePreferences is set, remove it.

cfg.CurvePreferences = nil // Go 1.24+ default includes X25519MLKEM768

Fixes by server: Any other OpenSSL-based server
(The exact config lines pqdoctor prints for nginx, Apache, HAProxy, Caddy, Node, Go, IIS, Java, mail servers, and the Cloudflare Tunnel fallback.)
Groups = X25519MLKEM768:X25519:prime256v1

Fixes by server: IIS / Windows Schannel
(The exact config lines pqdoctor prints for nginx, Apache, HAProxy, Caddy, Node, Go, IIS, Java, mail servers, and the Cloudflare Tunnel fallback.)
PQ key exchange in Schannel depends on the Windows Server version. If yours can’t offer ML-KEM yet, put Cloudflare Tunnel (or a PQ-capable reverse proxy) in front.

Fixes by server: Java
(The exact config lines pqdoctor prints for nginx, Apache, HAProxy, Caddy, Node, Go, IIS, Java, mail servers, and the Cloudflare Tunnel fallback.)
Hybrid ML-KEM in JSSE depends on the JDK release. Until yours has it, terminate TLS in a PQ-capable proxy (nginx or HAProxy on OpenSSL 3.5), or use Cloudflare Tunnel.

Fixes by server: Mail servers
(The exact config lines pqdoctor prints for nginx, Apache, HAProxy, Caddy, Node, Go, IIS, Java, mail servers, and the Cloudflare Tunnel fallback.)
Postfix, Dovecot, Exim and Exchange are on the Mail (STARTTLS) page.

Fixes by server: Can’t upgrade? Cloudflare Tunnel
(The exact config lines pqdoctor prints for nginx, Apache, HAProxy, Caddy, Node, Go, IIS, Java, mail servers, and the Cloudflare Tunnel fallback.)
Run cloudflared next to the server. The tunnel from the server to Cloudflare already uses post-quantum key agreement, so the hop that leaves your network is protected even if the server isn’t.

cloudflared tunnel run <tunnel-name>

Probes and wire format: Overview
(Exactly what pqdoctor sends - every ClientHello's groups, key shares, sizes and splits, the certificate probes, timeouts, retries and limits.)
This page documents pqdoctor 0.2.0’s network behaviour byte for byte (the seven probes, the certificate probes, the HTTP request and SSH are unchanged from 0.1.0; everything else here is new in 0.2.0 and opt-in or on only for one host), for anyone who needs to know exactly what reaches their server: network teams, IDS rule writers, and anyone reviewing the tool.

Probes and wire format: The seven ClientHellos
(Exactly what pqdoctor sends - every ClientHello's groups, key shares, sizes and splits, the certificate probes, timeouts, retries and limits.)
Every key-exchange probe is a TLS 1.3 ClientHello with the same base. Only the groups, the key share and how it’s sent change.

id | supported_groups | key_share | Sent
tls13Classical | X25519, P-256, P-384 | X25519 | Whole
pqOnly | X25519MLKEM768, X25519, P-256 | X25519MLKEM768 | Whole
pqPreference | X25519MLKEM768, X25519, P-256 | X25519 | Whole
kyberDraft | X25519Kyber768Draft00, X25519, P-256 | X25519Kyber768Draft00 | Whole
pqSplit | Same hello as pqOnly | X25519MLKEM768 | Split
bigClassicalSplit | X25519, P-256 | X25519, padded to pqOnly’s size | Split
nistOnly | P-256, P-384 | P-256 | Whole
The common base

Field | Value
Record version | 0x0301
legacy_version | 0x0303
Random, session ID | 32 bytes each
supported_versions | TLS 1.3, TLS 1.2
Cipher suites (15) | 1301 1302 1303 c02b c02f c02c c030 cca9 cca8 c013 c014 009c 009d 002f 0035
signature_algorithms | 0403 0804 0401 0503 0805 0501 0806 0601 0807
ALPN | h2, http/1.1. Left out under STARTTLS
SNI | The host name, lowercased. None for IP addresses
psk_key_exchange_modes | psk_dhe_ke
Extension order: server_name, extended_master_secret, renegotiation_info, supported_groups, ec_point_formats, signature_algorithms, ALPN, supported_versions, psk_key_exchange_modes, key_share, then padding last when used.

Groups and key shares

Probes and wire format: The seven ClientHellos
(Exactly what pqdoctor sends - every ClientHello's groups, key shares, sizes and splits, the certificate probes, timeouts, retries and limits.)
Group | Codepoint | Key share bytes
X25519 | 0x001D | 32
P-256 (secp256r1) | 0x0017 | 65
P-384 (secp384r1) | 0x0018 | 97
X25519MLKEM768 | 0x11EC | 1,216: ML-KEM-768 key (1,184) then X25519 (32)
X25519Kyber768Draft00 | 0x6399 | 1,216: X25519 (32) then the Kyber key (1,184)
| SecP256r1MLKEM768 | 0x11EB | 1,249: P-256 (65) then ML-KEM-768 (1,184) | | SecP384r1MLKEM1024 | 0x11ED | 1,665: P-384 (97) then ML-KEM-1024 (1,568) | | MLKEM512 / MLKEM768 / MLKEM1024 | 0x0200 / 0x0201 / 0x0202 | 800 / 1,184 / 1,568 | Codepoints are from IANA’s TLS Supported Groups registry; the share layouts from RFC 10024 (ML-KEM first only in X25519MLKEM768) and draft-ietf-tls-mlkem. The last five are only sent by the group survey.

The key shares are placeholders. The key-exchange probes only read the server’s first reply, so no shared secret is ever computed. The ML-KEM part is a valid encapsulation key with all-zero coefficients and a 32-byte seed, and the classical shares are fixed points. No probe does real cryptography, and none could complete a handshake.

Padding and splitting

bigClassicalSplit gets a padding extension that makes its handshake exactly as long as pqOnly’s (over 1,300 bytes). That’s the control: same size, same split, no PQ group.

Split sends the first 200 bytes of the record (including the 5-byte record header), flushes, waits 40 ms, then sends the rest. TCP_NODELAY is set, so the two writes go as separate TCP segments.

Probes and wire format: The certificate probes
(Exactly what pqdoctor sends - every ClientHello's groups, key shares, sizes and splits, the certificate probes, timeouts, retries and limits.)
Run only for one host by default (and in scans with --auth), and only when tls13Classical got a TLS 1.3 reply. They’re the one place pqdoctor does real cryptography.

|
Probe 1: “Classical schemes, then ML-DSA” | Probe 2: “Only ML-DSA schemes”
supported_versions | TLS 1.3 only | TLS 1.3 only
Groups and key share | X25519, with a real X25519 key | Same
Cipher suites | TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 only | Same
signature_algorithms | The common list, then 0904 0905 0906 | 0904 0905 0906 only
pqdoctor completes the X25519 exchange, runs the TLS 1.3 key schedule, decrypts the server’s Certificate and CertificateVerify, and hangs up. It never sends Finished. The two probes are 120 ms apart, and a response is capped at 512 KB.

Probes and wire format: Group survey
(Exactly what pqdoctor sends - every ClientHello's groups, key shares, sizes and splits, the certificate probes, timeouts, retries and limits.)
On for one host (--no-groups to skip), --groups for scans. One hello per group below, offering only that group in supported_groups and key_share, so a ServerHello that picks it means the server accepts it. Same base as the seven probes, sent whole, one at a time, 120 ms apart, retried once on silence. X25519MLKEM768’s answer is taken from pqOnly, so it’s 5 more connections:

SecP256r1MLKEM768, SecP384r1MLKEM1024, MLKEM512, MLKEM768, MLKEM1024.

A server that only accepts one of these gets pq-other-group. The SecP384r1MLKEM1024 hello is about 1.9 KB.

Probes and wire format: SLH-DSA probe
(Exactly what pqdoctor sends - every ClientHello's groups, key shares, sizes and splits, the certificate probes, timeouts, retries and limits.)
--slh-dsa: one more certificate probe like probe 2 above, with signature_algorithms = the 12 IANA-registered SLH-DSA schemes 0911–091C. IANA has no composite (ML-DSA + classical) signature codepoints, so none are offered. Merkle Tree Certificates aren’t checked.

Probes and wire format: Trust
(Exactly what pqdoctor sends - every ClientHello's groups, key shares, sizes and splits, the certificate probes, timeouts, retries and limits.)
No probe of its own for a TLS 1.3 server: it validates the chain certificate probe 1 decrypted. For a TLS 1.2-only server, one hello without supported_versions (TLS 1.2), read up to ServerHelloDone; the Certificate is plaintext there.

Probes and wire format: QUIC
(Exactly what pqdoctor sends - every ClientHello's groups, key shares, sizes and splits, the certificate probes, timeouts, retries and limits.)
pqdoctor quic or --quic: three exchanges on UDP, each a fresh QUIC connection (random 8-byte connection IDs):

|
supported_groups | key_share
Classical | X25519, P-256 | X25519
PQ only | X25519MLKEM768, X25519, P-256 | X25519MLKEM768
PQ preference | X25519MLKEM768, X25519, P-256 | X25519
The ClientHello: TLS 1.3 only, an empty legacy_session_id, suites 1301 1302 1303, ALPN h3, and quic_transport_parameters (extension 57) with max_idle_timeout 30 s, max_udp_payload_size 1472, initial_max_data 1 MiB, stream data 256 KiB, 100 streams each way, and initial_source_connection_id. It goes in CRYPTO frames in Initial packets (4-byte packet numbers, PADDING to exactly 1,200 bytes per datagram), two datagrams for the PQ hello. 3 s per exchange, retried once on a timeout.

Probes and wire format: DTLS
(Exactly what pqdoctor sends - every ClientHello's groups, key shares, sizes and splits, the certificate probes, timeouts, retries and limits.)
pqdoctor dtls or --dtls: three probes on UDP, each from a fresh socket. DTLSPlaintext records (record version 0xFEFF, epoch 0) with handshake fragments of at most 1,100 bytes. legacy_version 0xFEFD, an empty session ID and cookie, no ALPN.

|
supported_versions | Groups / key share
DTLS 1.3 / 1.2 classical | 0xFEFC, 0xFEFD | X25519, P-256, P-384 / X25519
DTLS 1.3 PQ | 0xFEFC, 0xFEFD | X25519MLKEM768, X25519, P-256 / X25519MLKEM768
DTLS 1.2 only | — | X25519, P-256, P-384
A HelloVerifyRequest or a HelloRetryRequest cookie is answered once, with the same random. 4 s per probe.

Probes and wire format: Audit
(Exactly what pqdoctor sends - every ClientHello's groups, key shares, sizes and splits, the certificate probes, timeouts, retries and limits.)
--audit, one at a time, 150 ms apart, retried once on silence:

5 version probes: legacy_version 0x0300 (record 0x0300), 0x0301, 0x0302 and 0x0303 without supported_versions, and TLS 1.3 through supported_versions.

51 suite probes: one TLS 1.2 suite each (see the list), read up to ServerKeyExchange / ServerHelloDone.

1 preference probe: the weakest and strongest accepted suites, weakest first.

Only ClientHellos. No exploit, padding-oracle, Heartbleed or renegotiation bytes.

Probes and wire format: Middlebox
(Exactly what pqdoctor sends - every ClientHello's groups, key shares, sizes and splits, the certificate probes, timeouts, retries and limits.)
--middlebox: 8 connections, see the variants. The splits are 40 ms apart with TCP_NODELAY.

Probes and wire format: Proxies
(Exactly what pqdoctor sends - every ClientHello's groups, key shares, sizes and splits, the certificate probes, timeouts, retries and limits.)
With --proxy, every TCP connection above first does CONNECT host:port HTTP/1.1 (http) or a SOCKS5 CONNECT (RFC 1928, with RFC 1929 credentials) to the proxy. The TLS bytes after it are unchanged. QUIC and DTLS don’t use the proxy.

Probes and wire format: Timing and retries
(Exactly what pqdoctor sends - every ClientHello's groups, key shares, sizes and splits, the certificate probes, timeouts, retries and limits.)
|
Value
Connect timeout | 5 s
Read timeout | 5 s, one deadline from after the hello is written
Gap between probes (and between addresses) | 120 ms
Retry | Once, after 700 ms, for a probe with no reply (timeout, reset, closed). A retry’s reply is kept only if it isn’t silent
Stop early | If the first probe can’t connect, the rest are skipped
Not TLS | Over 64 KiB without a ServerHello
STARTTLS upgrade | 10 s deadline. One upgrade first, then again before every probe

Probes and wire format: The HTTP request
(Exactly what pqdoctor sends - every ClientHello's groups, key shares, sizes and splits, the certificate probes, timeouts, retries and limits.)
One plain-HTTP request on port 80, to tailor the fixes:

HEAD / HTTP/1.1

Host: example.com

User-Agent: pqdoctor/0.4.0 (post-quantum TLS check; handshake-only)

Connection: close

3 s connect and read timeouts. Up to 8 KiB is read, stopping at the end of the headers.

--contact C adds ; contact: C inside the parentheses. --user-agent replaces it. A value with a line break is refused.

Skipped for IP addresses, with --no-http, under STARTTLS, and for any address but the first.

Probes and wire format: STARTTLS
(Exactly what pqdoctor sends - every ClientHello's groups, key shares, sizes and splits, the certificate probes, timeouts, retries and limits.)
Protocol | Commands sent
SMTP | EHLO pqdoctor.invalid, then STARTTLS
IMAP | pq1 STARTTLS
POP3 | STLS
FTP (0.2.0) | AUTH TLS → 234 (RFC 4217)
XMPP (0.2.0) | A jabber:client stream header to the host name, then <starttls xmlns='urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:xmpp-tls'/> → <proceed/>
LDAP (0.2.0) | ExtendedRequest 1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.20037, message ID 1 (31 bytes of BER) → resultCode 0
PostgreSQL (0.2.0) | SSLRequest (length 8, code 80877103) → S
MySQL (0.2.0) | Reads the server’s handshake, checks CLIENT_SSL, sends a 32-byte SSLRequest (sequence 1)
RDP (0.2.0) | TPKT + X.224 Connection Request with RDP_NEG_REQ, PROTOCOL_SSL | PROTOCOL_HYBRID → Connection Confirm; TLS follows (CredSSP is never reached)
Picked by port when --starttls isn’t given: 25 and 587 SMTP, 143 IMAP, 110 POP3, and in the CLI from 0.2.0 21 FTP, 5222 XMPP, 389 LDAP, 5432 PostgreSQL, 3306 MySQL, 3389 RDP. Each reads exactly the go-ahead’s bytes, so the next byte is the server’s TLS reply.

Probes and wire format: SSH
(Exactly what pqdoctor sends - every ClientHello's groups, key shares, sizes and splits, the certificate probes, timeouts, retries and limits.)
pqdoctor sends SSH-2.0-pqdoctor_0.2.0, reads the server’s identification and its first binary packet (KEXINIT), and closes the connection. Limits: 8 KiB of banner lines before the identification, a 255-byte identification, packets up to 256 KiB, and up to 8 IGNORE or DEBUG packets skipped. 5 s connect, read and write timeouts. Only the first address is checked.

|
Value

Probes and wire format: Identifying pqdoctor traffic
(Exactly what pqdoctor sends - every ClientHello's groups, key shares, sizes and splits, the certificate probes, timeouts, retries and limits.)
To recognise or filter pqdoctor on your network:

The User-Agent on port 80 starts with pqdoctor/.

The SSH client identification is SSH-2.0-pqdoctor_<version>.

From one source, a default single-host check is up to 7 TLS connections (plus up to 7 retries), 5 group-survey connections, 2 certificate connections and 1 HTTP request, all within a few seconds. --audit adds about 57, --middlebox 8, --slh-dsa 1.

QUIC Initials carry ALPN h3 and pqdoctor’s transport parameters; DTLS hellos carry no ALPN.

JSON output: Overview
(The full schema of pqdoctor's JSON - the one-host report, scan records, and the SSH report - with every field, type and value.)

Field names are camelCase. Enum values are camelCase (verdicts) or kebab-case (cause codes).

TLS numbers (versions, cipher suites, groups, extensions) are plain decimal integers. 772 is TLS 1.3 (0x0304). 4588 is X25519MLKEM768 (0x11EC).

Optional fields are null unless noted as omitted when empty.

Times are Unix milliseconds.

headline and cause are human sentences and can change between versions. Match on verdict and causeCode, which are stable.

(Every pqdoctor command, option, output format and exit status.)
0.4.0. Looks up a domain’s MX records and checks every mail server (at most 10, one at a time) on port 25 with the SMTP STARTTLS check. See A whole domain’s mail.

pqdoctor mail example.com

pqdoctor mail example.com --resolver 1.1.1.1 --json

pqdoctor mail example.com --submission # also 465 and 587 on the first MX

Option
--resolver IP | The DNS server for the MX lookup (IP or IP:port). Default: the system’s, from /etc/resolv.conf or ipconfig /all, else 1.1.1.1. The output says which
--submission | Also 465 and 587 on the first mail server
--all-addresses | Every address of each mail server, not just the first
The answer is for the domain: pq (every server that answered), mixed (naming which are and aren’t), notPq, or unreachable. Home and office networks often block outbound port 25; unreachable says so, and to run it from a server. After the first server can’t connect, the next gets one 2-second try; if that fails too, the rest are “not tried: port 25 looks blocked from here”.

No MX records means the domain itself is the mail server (“implicit MX”, RFC 5321 §5.1), and the output notes it. A null MX (RFC 7505) and a name that doesn’t exist are errors. Each server gets the light check: no certificate probe, group survey or fingerprint unless asked for.

Takes --format like one host; --json prints a MailReport. Exit status as for one host: 0 post-quantum, 1 mixed or not post-quantum, 2 unreachable or an error.

CLI reference: pqdoctor grade
(Every pqdoctor command, option, output format and exit status.)
0.4.0. One letter for a domain. It checks <domain>:443 and www.<domain>:443 with the one-host check (so the certificate probe too), and mail as pqdoctor mail does. When www.<domain> doesn’t resolve, it’s skipped and the output says so.

pqdoctor grade example.com

pqdoctor grade example.com --no-mail --json

Grade | When
A+ | A, plus mail post-quantum and the certificate side ready: it serves ML-DSA, or a whole ML-DSA-44 chain would still fit TCP’s first flight
A | Post-quantum everywhere; mail post-quantum or not checked
B | Post-quantum with a warning, or mail checked and not post-quantum
C | Some endpoints or addresses post-quantum, some not (mixed, apex vs www)
D | TLS 1.3, nothing post-quantum
F | No TLS 1.3 anywhere
Nothing reachable is “no grade”, not F. --no-mail leaves mail out, so the grade is then at most A. The text output has the letter, the summary, the reasons, what was and wasn’t checked (with the command that would check it) and each endpoint. --resolver is used for the mail part; --json prints a GradeReport.

Exit status: 0 for A+ to B, 1 for C to F, 2 for no grade.

CLI reference: pqdoctor ssh
(Every pqdoctor command, option, output format and exit status.)
Checks an SSH server’s key exchange offer, and flags post-quantum host-key algorithms from drafts. See SSH.

pqdoctor ssh github.com

pqdoctor ssh git.example.com:2222 --json

pqdoctor ssh ssh://git@example.org:7999 # the user name is ignored

Takes --format, --proxy, --history and --cbom. Exit status: 0 post-quantum, 1 draft-only or not post-quantum, 2 unreachable or an error.

CLI reference: pqdoctor quic / dtls
(Every pqdoctor command, option, output format and exit status.)
0.2.0. The key exchange over UDP. See QUIC and DTLS.

pqdoctor quic cloudflare.com # port 443

pqdoctor dtls vpn.example.org:4433 --json

Neither can go through --proxy (HTTP CONNECT and SOCKS5 CONNECT carry TCP only); with one set they exit 2 and say so. Exit status as for one host.

CLI reference: pqdoctor diff
(Every pqdoctor command, option, output format and exit status.)
0.2.0. Compares two history files: the newest record per target in each.

pqdoctor diff last-week.jsonl today.jsonl

pqdoctor diff old.jsonl new.jsonl --json

A target is fixed when it went from not post-quantum to post-quantum, regressed when it went the other way (and still answers), mixed (0.4.0) when it went from post-quantum to mixed, which isn’t a regression, changed when its verdict, cause or group changed otherwise, and added / removed when it’s in only one file. Exit status: 1 when something regressed, else 0 (a host that went mixed alone exits 0); 2 when a file can’t be read. See History, diff and CBOM.

CLI reference: pqdoctor fix
(Every pqdoctor command, option, output format and exit status.)
0.2.0. Puts the post-quantum group (or key exchange) first in a server’s config. See Fixing a config.

pqdoctor fix --config /etc/nginx/nginx.conf # a unified diff; nothing changes

pqdoctor fix --config /etc/nginx/nginx.conf --write # writes it, keeps nginx.conf.bak

pqdoctor fix --config /etc/ssh/sshd_config --write --host git.example.org

Option
--config PATH | The file. Required
--stack S | nginx, apache, haproxy, postfix, dovecot, sshd, caddy or iis, when pqdoctor can’t tell from the file
--write | Write the change, keeping the original as PATH.bak (or .bak.1, …), and print the test, reload and re-check commands
--host H | The server to put in the printed re-check command
It never reloads anything. Caddy and IIS have nothing to rewrite; for them it explains what to do instead.

CLI reference: pqdoctor agent
(Every pqdoctor command, option, output format and exit status.)
Runs inventory → scan → diff → push → tickets from an agent.toml, on a schedule. See Across a company for the config.

pqdoctor agent agent.toml --once # one cycle, then exit

pqdoctor agent install agent.toml --every 6h --dry-run # 0.4.0

pqdoctor agent status dc-east # 0.4.0

pqdoctor agent uninstall dc-east # 0.4.0

Option
--once | One cycle, then exit. Without it, the agent repeats every interval_minutes
--every N | install: how often, e.g. 30m, 6h, 1d. Default: the config’s interval_minutes; at least 5m. 0.4.0
--dry-run | install, uninstall, status: print the files and commands only. 0.4.0
0.4.0. install runs agent --once from the OS scheduler: Windows Task Scheduler, a systemd user timer, or launchd. uninstall <name> removes it and status <name> shows it; the name is the config’s name. The agent re-checks a non-PQ answer once and doesn’t report mixed as a regression.

(Every pqdoctor command, option, output format and exit status.)
0.2.0.

pqdoctor completions bash > /etc/bash_completion.d/pqdoctor

pqdoctor completions zsh > "${fpath[1]}/_pqdoctor"

pqdoctor completions fish > ~/.config/fish/completions/pqdoctor.fish

pqdoctor completions powershell >> $PROFILE

pqdoctor man > /usr/local/share/man/man1/pqdoctor.1

(Every pqdoctor command, option, output format and exit status.)
0.2.0. Long options as key = value lines, read before the command line, so the command line wins. true turns a flag on, false leaves it out.

~/.config/pqdoctor/config
# %APPDATA%\pqdoctor\config on Windows; $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/pqdoctor/config if set

contact = security@example.org

PQDOCTOR_CONFIG names another file; --no-config skips it. A line that isn’t key = value exits 64, naming the line.

Format | One host | Scan
text | The report as a terminal reads it | TSV, a line per host
json | The report, pretty-printed | A record per line

Stream | Gets

Colour is used only when stdout is a terminal and NO_COLOR isn’t set, so piping and redirecting give plain text.

Scan TSV

host port verdict cause group stack headline

Scan summary (stderr)

(Every pqdoctor command, option, output format and exit status.)
Code | One host, ssh, quic, dtls, mail | grade | scan | diff
0 | Post-quantum | A+ to B | Completed | Nothing regressed
1 | Not post-quantum, mixed, TLS 1.2 only, broken, or draft-only | C to F | — | Something regressed

Verify by hand: Overview
(Confirm any pqdoctor verdict yourself with OpenSSL 3.5 or OpenSSH, independent of pqdoctor's own probes.)
Every pqdoctor report ends with a command that checks the same thing with standard tools. Use it to confirm a verdict, or after applying a fix.

Verify by hand: Key exchange, with OpenSSL 3.5+
(Confirm any pqdoctor verdict yourself with OpenSSL 3.5 or OpenSSH, independent of pqdoctor's own probes.)
Offer only X25519MLKEM768. A post-quantum server completes the handshake with it. Any other server fails.

openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com -groups X25519MLKEM768 </dev/null 2>&1 | grep -i 'group'

Post-quantum: the output names the negotiated group, X25519MLKEM768.

Not post-quantum: the handshake fails, typically with a handshake failure alert.

This needs OpenSSL 3.5 or newer (openssl version), the first release with ML-KEM. Older OpenSSL doesn’t know the group and refuses to run.

For mail, add -starttls smtp, imap or pop3. For an IP address, leave out -servername. pqdoctor’s report already prints the right variant.

TLS 1.2 only

openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -tls1_3 </dev/null

A TLS 1.2-only server answers with a protocol_version alert.

section: Is this how pqdoctor was checked?
text:
Verify by hand: Is this how pqdoctor was checked?
(Confirm any pqdoctor verdict yourself with OpenSSL 3.5 or OpenSSH, independent of pqdoctor's own probes.)
Yes. The accuracy checks used exactly this test, through Node 24’s OpenSSL 3.5.5: a completed PQ-only handshake proves support. pqdoctor agreed 59 / 59 on real sites where OpenSSL gave a definite answer.

One caution from that work: OpenSSL counts any later alert as a failure. receptivity.io picked X25519MLKEM768 in its ServerHello, then failed later on an SNI problem, so the plain OpenSSL test said “no” while the key exchange was in fact post-quantum. If OpenSSL fails, look at where.

Verify by hand: ML-DSA, with OpenSSL 3.5+
(Confirm any pqdoctor verdict yourself with OpenSSL 3.5 or OpenSSH, independent of pqdoctor's own probes.)
openssl s_client -connect origin.example.com:443 -sigalgs mldsa44 -brief </dev/null

A server with an ML-DSA-44 certificate completes and prints Signature type: mldsa44. One without it fails.

Verify by hand: SSH, with OpenSSH
(Confirm any pqdoctor verdict yourself with OpenSSL 3.5 or OpenSSH, independent of pqdoctor's own probes.)
ssh -vv -o BatchMode=yes -o StrictHostKeyChecking=yes -o UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null -o GlobalKnownHostsFile=/dev/null github.com 2>&1 | grep -E 'kex: algorithm|KEX algorithms'

With no known host keys, ssh stops right after the key exchange, before offering any key, so it can’t log in. Look for kex: algorithm: mlkem768x25519-sha256. This needs an OpenSSH client with that method: 9.9 or newer.

Certificate trust: Overview
(pqdoctor checks the certificate chain against Mozilla's roots — trusted, expired, name-mismatch, untrusted-root or self-signed.)
0.2.0
New in pqdoctor 0.2.0. On by default for one host. It uses the chain from the certificate check, so --no-auth turns it off too; --no-trust skips only this.

The chain the certificate check reads is validated the way a browser would:

a path from the leaf, through the intermediates the server sent, to a root in Mozilla’s root store (the webpki-roots crate);

every certificate within its validity period, right now;

the leaf valid for the host name you checked, and for server authentication.

Trust Trusted certificate (trusted)

Chains to GTS Root R4 and is valid for cloudflare.com until 2026-12-04T23:29:33Z.

Certificate trust: Verdicts
(pqdoctor checks the certificate chain against Mozilla's roots — trusted, expired, name-mismatch, untrusted-root or self-signed.)
trust.verdict | Meaning
trusted | Valid for this name, chains to a Mozilla root
expired | A certificate in the chain is past its notAfter
not-yet-valid | A certificate isn’t valid yet (or this machine’s clock is wrong)
name-mismatch | The leaf doesn’t cover the host name
untrusted-root | The chain doesn’t reach a Mozilla root: a private CA, or a missing intermediate
self-signed | The leaf signs itself
unverifiable | The chain uses a signature pqdoctor can’t verify, e.g. ML-DSA or SLH-DSA (no public root uses them yet)
When several apply, verdict is the most important one (issuer first, then time, then name) and problems lists them all.

Checked against badssl.com on 2026-10-15: expired., wrong.host., self-signed. and untrusted-root.badssl.com each got their verdict, and sha256.badssl.com was trusted (an RSA chain to ISRG Root X1).

Certificate trust: How
(pqdoctor checks the certificate chain against Mozilla's roots — trusted, expired, name-mismatch, untrusted-root or self-signed.)
TLS 1.3 servers: the chain comes from the certificate check, which decrypts the server’s first flight. No extra connection.

TLS 1.2-only servers: the Certificate message is plaintext, so one TLS 1.2 hello reads it, up to ServerHelloDone, and hangs up.

Signatures are checked with rustls-webpki and pure-Rust code (the RustCrypto p256, p384 and rsa crates and ed25519-dalek): ECDSA P-256 / P-384, RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 and PSS (2048–8192 bits), and Ed25519. No C crypto library is linked.

There is no revocation check. No OCSP or CRL request is made, so the check stays handshake-only.

The result is the report’s trust field. The pqdoctor crate’s trust feature (on by default) builds it; the checker on Cloudflare’s network (pqdoctor web) is built without it.

ML-DSA readiness: Overview
(Does the server serve a post-quantum (ML-DSA) certificate? What pqdoctor checks, and what it can and can't tell.)
Post-quantum key exchange protects today’s traffic from being recorded now and decrypted later. Authentication is the second half: the server’s certificate and its signature on the handshake. The post-quantum signature standard is ML-DSA.

Cloudflare accepts ML-DSA certificates on the hop from Cloudflare to the origin (blog, 2026-07-29). Browsers don’t take ML-DSA certificates from public CAs yet.

ML-DSA readiness: What pqdoctor checks
(Does the server serve a post-quantum (ML-DSA) certificate? What pqdoctor checks, and what it can and can't tell.)
TLS 1.3 encrypts the Certificate message, so pqdoctor has to do one real exchange to read it. It completes an X25519 exchange and runs the TLS 1.3 key schedule (AES-128-GCM) just far enough to decrypt the Certificate and CertificateVerify, then hangs up. It never sends Finished.

It makes two such connections:

Classical schemes, then ML-DSA. This is the chain today’s clients get, and it shows whether listing ML-DSA codepoints breaks anything.

Only ML-DSA schemes. Does the server sign with ML-DSA when that’s all the client accepts?

The codepoints are mldsa44 0x0904, mldsa65 0x0905 and mldsa87 0x0906, per draft-ietf-tls-mldsa-06 and the IANA registry.

ML-DSA readiness: Results
(Does the server serve a post-quantum (ML-DSA) certificate? What pqdoctor checks, and what it can and can't tell.)
ml-dsa | Headline | Means
serves | Serves an ML-DSA certificate | Offered only ML-DSA, it signs with ML-DSA
no-cert | No ML-DSA certificate | Offered only ML-DSA, it refuses cleanly
ignores-offer | No ML-DSA certificate (and the offer is ignored) | Offered only ML-DSA, it still signs with a classical key, so an ML-DSA-only client would fail
rejects-codepoints | Breaks on ML-DSA signature algorithms | Listing ML-DSA next to classical schemes breaks the handshake. TLS requires unknown schemes to be ignored
unknown | ML-DSA readiness unknown | Neither probe got far enough
What no-cert doesn’t say
Refusing cleanly is what any correct TLS stack does when it has no ML-DSA certificate. So no-cert doesn’t show whether the stack could serve ML-DSA. Early versions said “Ready for ML-DSA” here. That overclaimed, and it was changed.

ML-DSA readiness: The fix: dual certificates
(Does the server serve a post-quantum (ML-DSA) certificate? What pqdoctor checks, and what it can and can't tell.)
Serving ML-DSA needs a TLS library that has it (OpenSSL 3.5+) and an ML-DSA certificate. Configure it as a second certificate and key next to the current one. The server picks per client, so today’s clients keep the classical certificate.

openssl genpkey -algorithm ML-DSA-44 -out mldsa.key

# issue mldsa.crt from your CA, then in nginx add a second pair:

ssl_certificate mldsa.crt;

ssl_certificate_key mldsa.key;

Public CAs don’t issue ML-DSA certificates yet, so issue it from your own CA or an origin CA. Flarebox makes one on your machine.

ML-DSA readiness: Shown in the fix lab
(Does the server serve a post-quantum (ML-DSA) certificate? What pqdoctor checks, and what it can and can't tell.)
An OpenSSL 3.5 server with one ECDSA P-256 certificate was reported “No ML-DSA certificate”. Given an ML-DSA-44 certificate next to the ECDSA one, it served ML-DSA to ML-DSA clients, and a classical-only client still got ecdsa_secp256r1_sha256. The chain grew from 364 to 3,919 bytes.

ML-DSA readiness: Real output
(Does the server serve a post-quantum (ML-DSA) certificate? What pqdoctor checks, and what it can and can't tell.)
pqdoctor github.com (authentication)
Authentication No ML-DSA certificate

Leaf: ec-p256 key, signed ecdsa-sha256. Listing ML-DSA schemes doesn't break it, and offered only ML-DSA it refuses cleanly — what any correct TLS stack does, so this doesn't show whether its stack could serve ML-DSA. The chain is 2737 bytes.

ml-dsa: no-cert

leaf github.com ec-p256 signed ecdsa-sha256 1009 B

↑ Sectigo Public Server Authenticat… ec-p256 signed ecdsa-sha384 867 B

↑ Sectigo Public Server Authenticat… ec-p384 signed ecdsa-sha384 842 B

On by default for one host. In a scan, --auth turns it on (two more connections a host). --no-auth skips it.

section: SLH-DSA, composite signatures, Merkle Tree Certificates
text:
ML-DSA readiness: SLH-DSA, composite signatures, Merkle Tree Certificates
(Does the server serve a post-quantum (ML-DSA) certificate? What pqdoctor checks, and what it can and can't tell.)
0.2.0
New in pqdoctor 0.2.0.

SLH-DSA (FIPS 205): --slh-dsa adds a probe offering only the 12 SLH-DSA schemes IANA registered (0x0911–0x091C, draft-reddy-tls-slhdsa). signatures.slhdsa is serves, no-cert, ignores-offer or unknown. Certificate keys and signatures are named by NIST CSOR OID, e.g. slh-dsa-sha2-128s (2.16.840.1.101.3.4.3.20), and the pre-hash hash-slh-dsa-* OIDs too.

Composite ML-DSA + classical signatures: IANA had registered no TLS codepoints for them on 2026-10-15, so pqdoctor offers none rather than guess. signatures.composite says so.

Merkle Tree Certificates are experimental; pqdoctor reports them as not checked: experimental.

The chain itself is checked against Mozilla’s roots by Certificate trust. An ML-DSA or SLH-DSA chain comes back unverifiable there: no public root uses them yet.

Post-quantum TLS in 5 minutes: Overview
(The background for everything else here - key exchange vs authentication, hybrid ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and why post-quantum hellos break old middleboxes.)
This page is the background you need for the rest of the docs. If you already know what X25519MLKEM768 is and why a ClientHello gets split, skip to How pqdoctor works.

Post-quantum TLS in 5 minutes: Two separate problems
(The background for everything else here - key exchange vs authentication, hybrid ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and why post-quantum hellos break old middleboxes.)
A TLS connection does two cryptographic jobs, and post-quantum migration touches both.

|
Key exchange | Authentication
What it does | Agrees a secret key for this connection | Proves the server is who it says it is
Classical today | X25519 or ECDHE with P-256 | RSA or ECDSA certificates and signatures
Post-quantum | ML-KEM (FIPS 203), usually as a hybrid with X25519 | ML-DSA (FIPS 204) certificates and signatures
The quantum risk | Harvest now, decrypt later: traffic recorded today can be decrypted once a large quantum computer exists | A forged signature only matters at the time of the connection, so this one can wait longer
Urgency | Now | Later; browsers don’t accept ML-DSA from public CAs yet
That’s why pqdoctor’s main verdict is about key exchange, and the ML-DSA check is a separate section of the report.

Post-quantum TLS in 5 minutes: Hybrid key exchange: X25519MLKEM768
(The background for everything else here - key exchange vs authentication, hybrid ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and why post-quantum hellos break old middleboxes.)
The post-quantum key exchange deployed on the web today is a hybrid: the client and server do an X25519 exchange and an ML-KEM-768 exchange together, and combine both secrets. If either one holds, the connection is safe. So a hybrid is never weaker than today’s X25519.

In TLS 1.3 it’s a named group, like X25519 or P-256:

Group | Codepoint | Status
X25519MLKEM768 | 0x11EC | The standard hybrid. What browsers and Cloudflare use
X25519Kyber768Draft00 | 0x6399 | The pre-standard draft. Browsers have dropped it
X25519 | 0x001D | Classical
secp256r1 (P-256) | 0x0017 | Classical (NIST)
A server is post-quantum, for pqdoctor’s purposes, when it negotiates X25519MLKEM768.

section: How a server picks a group
text:
Post-quantum TLS in 5 minutes: How a server picks a group
(The background for everything else here - key exchange vs authentication, hybrid ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and why post-quantum hellos break old middleboxes.)
In TLS 1.3 the client sends a list of groups it supports and one or more key shares: public keys for some of those groups, so the server can answer in one round trip.

If the server supports a group the client sent a share for, it answers with a ServerHello for that group.

If it prefers a group the client listed but didn’t send a share for, it answers with a HelloRetryRequest asking the client to try again with that group.

That second rule is how pqdoctor tells “supports ML-KEM” apart from “prefers ML-KEM”. It sends an X25519 share with ML-KEM listed first. A server that asks for a retry with ML-KEM prefers it (pq-preferred). One that just picks X25519 doesn’t (pq). Browsers send both shares, so the difference rarely matters for them, but it does for clients that only send X25519.

Post-quantum TLS in 5 minutes: Why post-quantum hellos are big
(The background for everything else here - key exchange vs authentication, hybrid ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and why post-quantum hellos break old middleboxes.)
An ML-KEM-768 public key is 1,184 bytes, so the X25519MLKEM768 key share is 1,216 bytes. A ClientHello carrying it is well over a thousand bytes, often more than fits in one TCP segment, so it’s split across two segments.

Most servers don’t care. But some load balancers, firewalls and TLS-inspecting appliances only look at the first segment, or can’t reassemble a ClientHello that spans two. They drop the connection or reset it. That’s protocol ossification, and it’s why pqdoctor sends a split PQ hello and a classical hello padded to the same size and split the same way. If both die, the size and split are the problem (large-hello-dropped). If only the PQ one dies, the codepoint is (pq-group-rejected).

Post-quantum TLS in 5 minutes: Where Cloudflare fits
(The background for everything else here - key exchange vs authentication, hybrid ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and why post-quantum hellos break old middleboxes.)
A request through Cloudflare has two TLS hops:

browser ──TLS──▶ Cloudflare edge ──TLS──▶ your origin server

(1) (2)

Browser to edge is Cloudflare’s side, and it’s already post-quantum for most browser traffic.

Edge to origin depends on your server. Cloudflare’s “Automatic key exchange” uses post-quantum to the origin when the origin supports it, so whether hop 2 is post-quantum comes down to your origin’s TLS stack and config. That’s what pqdoctor diagnoses, and what Flarebox checks for every origin behind your zones.

If you can’t upgrade the origin, Cloudflare Tunnel replaces hop 2 with a tunnel that already uses post-quantum key agreement.

Post-quantum TLS in 5 minutes: Authentication: ML-DSA
(The background for everything else here - key exchange vs authentication, hybrid ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and why post-quantum hellos break old middleboxes.)
For hop 2, Cloudflare accepts ML-DSA certificates from your origin (Cloudflare blog, 2026-07-29), once the zone’s Custom Origin Trust Store holds the CA. ML-DSA-44 is the recommended size. Its public keys and signatures are much bigger than ECDSA’s: in the fix lab, adding an ML-DSA-44 certificate grew the chain from 364 to 3,919 bytes. The usual setup is dual certificates: the server keeps its ECDSA certificate for today’s clients and serves ML-DSA to clients that ask for it.

See ML-DSA readiness and ML-DSA origin certificates.

Post-quantum TLS in 5 minutes: SSH
(The background for everything else here - key exchange vs authentication, hybrid ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and why post-quantum hellos break old middleboxes.)
SSH has its own post-quantum key exchange methods: mlkem768x25519-sha256 (OpenSSH 9.9+, the default from 10.0) and sntrup761x25519-sha512 (OpenSSH’s default from 9.0). See SSH.

Post-quantum TLS in 5 minutes: Deadlines
(The background for everything else here - key exchange vs authentication, hybrid ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and why post-quantum hellos break old middleboxes.)
Governments have set dates for the migration: NIST, the NSA’s CNSA 2.0, the EU, the UK NCSC and Australia’s ASD. Flarebox lists 12 dated milestones, each with its source, against your zone’s results. See Deadlines.

FAQ: Post-quantum basics
(Common questions about post-quantum TLS, pqdoctor's results, scanning safely, fixing servers, certificates, CI, rolling it out across an organization, and Flarebox.)
What does “post-quantum” mean here?

That a server negotiates a key exchange a quantum computer can’t break. In TLS today that’s a hybrid group: X25519MLKEM768 combines the classical X25519 with ML-KEM-768 (NIST FIPS 203). pqdoctor reports a server as post-quantum when it negotiates a hybrid or pure ML-KEM group.

Quantum computers that break TLS don’t exist yet. Why act now?

Because traffic recorded today can be decrypted later (“harvest now, decrypt later”). Anything with a long confidentiality life (health, finance, credentials, private messages) is exposed by every classical handshake made from now on. Key exchange is the part that protects it, and it’s also the part that’s ready to switch today.

Why hybrid and not ML-KEM alone?

Hybrid is at least as strong as X25519 even if a weakness were found in ML-KEM, and it’s what browsers and Cloudflare deploy. Pure ML-KEM groups exist (MLKEM768, MLKEM1024); pqdoctor’s group survey reports whether a server accepts them.

My site is behind Cloudflare. Isn’t it post-quantum already?

The visitor’s connection to Cloudflare is. The connection from Cloudflare to your origin is a separate TLS connection, and it’s post-quantum only if your origin’s TLS library has ML-KEM and its configuration allows it. That hop is what pqdoctor and Flarebox’s Post-quantum tab check. The same applies to any CDN or load balancer in front of a server.

Chrome’s security panel says the connection uses ML-KEM. Why does pqdoctor say no?

Chrome is describing its connection to whatever it reached first, usually a CDN edge. pqdoctor checks the server you named: if that’s your origin (by its own address or name), the answer can differ. Check the edge and the origin separately to see both hops.

Does post-quantum TLS slow things down?

Slightly more bytes, not noticeably more time: an X25519MLKEM768 key share is 1,216 bytes instead of 32, so the ClientHello grows by about a kilobyte and the server’s reply by about the same. ML-KEM itself is fast. Certificates are different: ML-DSA signatures are large, see the certificate questions.

FAQ: Results and accuracy
(Common questions about post-quantum TLS, pqdoctor's results, scanning safely, fixing servers, certificates, CI, rolling it out across an organization, and Flarebox.)
What do the verdicts mean?

Post-quantum: it negotiated an ML-KEM group. Not post-quantum: TLS works, but the key exchange is classical. Unreachable: no TLS answer at all (down, firewalled, or only reachable from inside). Each result also has one cause code, such as no-mlkem or tls12-only, that says why.

A host gives different answers from run to run, or from two machines. Why?

Usually several servers behind one name: a load balancer, DNS round-robin, or a different server per region. pqdoctor checks every address of a host (up to six) and lists them when they disagree. From two machines you may also reach different servers (GeoDNS, anycast) or be blocked differently. Pin one with host:port on an IP to compare like with like.

How sure is the “why, one level down” answer?

Each answer has a confidence (high, medium or low) and the evidence behind it, so you can disagree on the facts. It comes from which classical groups the server accepts, the Server header, version banners and provider address ranges. When a hand-set group list hides the library version the answer is unknown; running pqdoctor <host> --local on the server reads the real versions, and local evidence always wins.

Can I check internal servers, mail servers or SSH?

Yes. Run pqdoctor from inside the network for internal names. Mail servers are checked over STARTTLS (mail.example.com:587, or :25), and so are IMAP, POP3, FTP, XMPP, LDAP, PostgreSQL, MySQL and RDP by port. pqdoctor ssh host checks an SSH server’s key exchange, pqdoctor quic host checks HTTP/3.

Does it work through a corporate proxy?
