FAQ: Scanning safely
(Common questions about post-quantum TLS, pqdoctor's results, scanning safely, fixing servers, certificates, CI, rolling it out across an organization, and Flarebox.)
How many hosts can one scan check?

There’s no fixed limit: pqdoctor scan takes a list of any length, from a file or standard input, and checks 4 hosts at once by default (--concurrency goes up to 32). Each host is checked on its own and written as soon as it’s done, so a longer list only takes longer; what’s capped is how fast the scan goes, to stay gentle on the servers. The study’s 5,139 hosts took about 80 minutes at the defaults. For long lists, write results with --out and add --resume, so an interrupted scan picks up where it stopped. See How many hosts.

How fast does a scan go, and can I make it gentler?

By default 4 hosts at a time and at most 2 new hosts a second. --concurrency and --rate change that; --exclude keeps hosts or whole domains out, and --skip-ranges skips addresses in networks you name (for example a CDN’s).

Could a scan set off our intrusion detection?

It sends ordinary TLS ClientHellos and reads one reply each, the same as any client connecting. A whole scan looks like a burst of short connections from one address, which some systems notice. Tell your security operations team first and set contact = … in the config file so the User-Agent of the one HTTP request names you.

Does pqdoctor store anything?

Only what you ask for: --out writes scan results, --history appends checks for pqdoctor diff, --cbom writes a bill of materials. Nothing is sent anywhere unless you run push (to your own fleet) or tickets --apply (to GitHub).

FAQ: Fixing
(Common questions about post-quantum TLS, pqdoctor's results, scanning safely, fixing servers, certificates, CI, rolling it out across an organization, and Flarebox.)
Which TLS libraries can do it?

OpenSSL 3.5 or newer, current BoringSSL and AWS-LC, Go 1.24+, rustls 0.23.27+ with aws-lc-rs, and Node 22.20+ or 24.5+. A server is only as new as the library it’s built against: nginx built on OpenSSL 3.0 can’t, whatever openssl version says on the same machine.

Which servers can pqdoctor fix edit?

nginx, Apache, HAProxy, Postfix, Dovecot and OpenSSH get a diff (and --apply applies it with a config test, a reload, a re-check from outside, and rollback on any failure). Caddy and IIS get an explanation instead, because their configuration works differently.

We can’t upgrade the library this quarter. Now what?

Put a post-quantum sidecar in front: pqdoctor sidecar host writes the configuration for a Cloudflare Tunnel (cloudflared, when the name is in a Cloudflare zone you manage) or for Caddy 2.10+ terminating TLS on the same machine. The library upgrade can follow on its own schedule.

The fix is applied but the check still says no.

Common reasons: the server wasn’t reloaded (or another worker still serves the old config); another server behind the same name wasn’t changed (check the address list); a load balancer or CDN in front terminates TLS itself; or the binary is linked against an older library than you expect (nginx -V). In Flarebox, Fix applied… re-checks and keeps the before and after.

FAQ: Certificates and ML-DSA
(Common questions about post-quantum TLS, pqdoctor's results, scanning safely, fixing servers, certificates, CI, rolling it out across an organization, and Flarebox.)
Do we need ML-DSA certificates now?

Not urgently. Certificates protect against impersonation at connection time, so recorded traffic isn’t at risk the way it is for key exchange, and browsers don’t yet accept ML-DSA certificates from public certificate authorities. Plan for it: measure your chains, keep them short, and try ML-DSA where you control both ends, such as the Cloudflare-to-origin hop.

Why does chain size matter?

An ML-DSA-44 public key is 1,312 bytes and a signature 2,420 bytes, so every certificate grows by about 3.7 KB. A server’s first reply that no longer fits QUIC’s 3,600-byte limit or TCP’s initial window (about 14.6 KB) costs an extra round trip on every new connection. pqdoctor projects each chain to ML-DSA and says which limit it would cross and what to trim first.

FAQ: CI and automation
(Common questions about post-quantum TLS, pqdoctor's results, scanning safely, fixing servers, certificates, CI, rolling it out across an organization, and Flarebox.)
What do the exit codes mean?

For one host (and ssh, quic, dtls): 0 post-quantum, 1 not post-quantum, 2 unreachable or an error. pqdoctor diff exits 1 when something regressed. Bad arguments exit 64.

Which output formats are there?

--format text (the default), json, csv, html (one self-contained file), sarif (for code scanning) and junit (for test dashboards). The JSON shape is documented in the reference, and new fields are only ever added.

Can CI fail only when something gets worse?

Yes. The GitHub Action has fail-on: regression, which fails only when a host that was post-quantum in the last run isn’t now. Outside GitHub, keep the last run’s results and use pqdoctor diff old.jsonl new.jsonl, which exits 1 on a regression.

FAQ: pqdoctor
(Common questions about post-quantum TLS, pqdoctor's results, scanning safely, fixing servers, certificates, CI, rolling it out across an organization, and Flarebox.)
Is it safe to run against servers I don’t own?

pqdoctor is handshake-only: it reads each server’s first reply and never completes a key-exchange handshake or sends application data. A single check is a handful of short connections and one HEAD / request. That said, scanning other people’s servers is your responsibility. Identify yourself with --contact, keep the default pacing, and honour opt-outs. See Scanning a list.

Why does my server say no-mlkem when I enabled post-quantum?

Usually the TLS library underneath is older than you think: nginx or Apache linked against OpenSSL 3.0, say, even if openssl version on the box says 3.5. Check what the server itself is linked against (nginx -V, httpd -V). Or a curve list set by hand leaves X25519MLKEM768 out. See no-mlkem.

pqdoctor and OpenSSL disagree. Which is right?

Look at where OpenSSL failed. pqdoctor reads the ServerHello, so it answers “which group did the server pick”. OpenSSL completes the whole handshake, so a later problem (a missing SNI certificate, say) fails it even when the key exchange was post-quantum. In the accuracy checks, that’s what explained the disagreements. See Accuracy.

What’s the difference between pq and pq-preferred?

Both are post-quantum. pq-preferred servers pick ML-KEM even when the client’s first key share is classical, by asking it to retry. pq servers only use ML-KEM when the client offers it first. Browsers offer both shares, so the difference rarely matters for them.

Why is the origin “unreachable” when the site works?

Your browser reaches Cloudflare, not the origin. A well-configured origin behind Cloudflare only accepts Cloudflare’s IPs, so from anywhere else it’s unreachable. Check it from inside its network, or let Flarebox connect to the origin address directly.

Does it check post-quantum certificates?

Yes, separately from key exchange: the ML-DSA check says whether the server serves an ML-DSA certificate. It’s on by default for one host; --auth turns it on for scans. It also projects the chain to ML-DSA and says whether the server’s first flight would still fit QUIC’s 3,600-byte limit and TCP’s initial window (about 14.6 KB), or cost a round trip.

How do I know a download is genuine?

pqdoctor comes only from npm and from its own APT repository, apt.pqdoctor.com. npm checks every package against the registry’s hash, and apt checks the repository’s signature (key fingerprint 0166 60F0 74FB 0329 78E2 5ECB 29DD A235 4EBB 4DFA). Flarebox’s installers have a SHA256SUMS.txt on the Downloads page.

Is there a Linux or macOS build?

Yes. npm install -g pqdoctor installs a universal macOS binary (Apple silicon and Intel, macOS 11 or later), static Linux binaries for x86_64 and arm64, or the Windows one. The GitHub Action’s own tests run it on Linux x64, Linux arm64, macOS and Windows against live hosts.

What does it send exactly?

Every byte is documented in Probes and wire format.

FAQ: For organizations
(Common questions about post-quantum TLS, pqdoctor's results, scanning safely, fixing servers, certificates, CI, rolling it out across an organization, and Flarebox.)
How would a company roll this out?

In five steps: inventory every endpoint (pqdoctor inventory from certificate transparency, DNS zones, Cloudflare, Kubernetes, Terraform and AWS), scan from outside and inside with the fingerprint, route each finding to its owner (owners.toml and pqdoctor tickets), track it in one dashboard (the fleet), and gate CI so it can’t regress (the GitHub Action). The Across a company guide shows each step.

Do we have to install anything on our servers?

No. Everything works from outside. The agent runs the whole cycle on a schedule from inside a network, for internal names and origins that only accept your CDN. pqdoctor <host> --local on a server is optional: it reads the server software’s versions and sharpens the classification.

Is it safe to scan our production estate?

The probes are handshake-only: each reads the server’s first reply and hangs up, with no application data and no completed handshake. Scans are paced (4 hosts in flight, 2 new hosts a second by default). Set contact in the config file so your operations team can recognise the traffic, and keep third-party names out with --exclude.

What is the fleet? Is it a hosted service?

How do teams find out what to fix?

pqdoctor tickets files one GitHub issue per non-post-quantum host for the team that owns it, with the cause, the class (config, library or provider), the confidence and the exact next command. Re-runs update the same issue, and it closes itself once the host is post-quantum. For Jira, --jira-csv writes an importable file.

Which hosts should we fix first?

The ones that move the most traffic per hour of work. pqdoctor plan groups hosts by TLS terminator (one ingress controller can serve hundreds of names), weights them by traffic (your own analytics or a rank list) and orders the actions by gain per effort, with a bound on what any plan could reach. See Plan.

Can it change our servers?

Only when you ask. pqdoctor fix --apply changes a server config after a typed confirmation, runs the server’s own config test, reloads, re-checks from outside, and rolls everything back if any step fails or the host still isn’t post-quantum. We don’t use GitHub. Does it still fit?

Yes. The CLI fits any CI: exit codes (0 post-quantum, 1 not, 2 unreachable), --format junit and --format sarif, and pqdoctor diff exits 1 on a regression. Tickets export to Jira as CSV. The fleet takes runs from anything that can make an HTTPS request.

Does X25519MLKEM768 satisfy CNSA 2.0?

No. CNSA 2.0 (US national security systems) specifies ML-KEM-1024 and ML-DSA-87. The group survey reports whether a server accepts SecP384r1MLKEM1024 or pure ML-KEM-1024; every other organization is well served by X25519MLKEM768, which is what browsers and Cloudflare use.

What evidence can we give auditors?

Fleet CSV exports and the trend; a CycloneDX 1.6 cryptographic bill of materials from any scan (--cbom FILE); Flarebox’s readiness report (one PDF per Cloudflare zone, citing the public NIST, NSA, NCSC, ASD and EU deadlines); and closed issues as a record of each fix.

What does it cost, and who supports it?

Nothing: pqdoctor and Flarebox, including the GitHub Action and the fleet, are free to use. It’s an independent project; questions and bugs go to GitHub issues.
